A Spanish research team has published preliminary results from a clinical trial that measures the effect of cannabidiol on people living with chronic pain. The trial, carried out in three hospitals in Madrid and Valencia, followed 84 patients with fibromyalgia for twelve weeks. Participants received a standardised oral cannabidiol preparation or a placebo, and the primary outcome was a validated pain intensity scale. The authors report a modest reduction in the cannabidiol group compared with placebo, with the largest differences appearing after eight weeks of treatment. Adverse events were mostly mild and included drowsiness and dry mouth, and no serious events were attributed to the intervention. The research group notes that the sample size limits the strength of the conclusions and that the follow-up period was too short to assess whether the effect persists. They also point out that the preparation used in the trial is not the same as products sold in pharmacies or online, which makes direct comparisons difficult. An accompanying editorial argues that the field needs larger multicentre trials with standardised products and longer follow-up before clinical guidance can change. The editorial also stresses that patients should not change their treatment on the basis of a single study, and that clinicians should discuss expectations openly. Funding for the trial came from a national research agency and none of the authors declared a conflict of interest related to the cannabis industry.
